To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

hyperglycemia is a primary cause of neuropathy in the insulin-dependent diabetic rat, and that the morphologic expression in human diabetic neuropathies may vary depending on the duration and severity of the diabetes, the presence or absence of insulin-dependence, the age of the patient and other factors.
hyperglycemia is a major cause of neuropathy in both insulin-dependent and noninsulin-dependent diabetes and that the morphologic expression is different in the two types of diabetes.

hyperglycemia, acting through a sequence of metabolic and functional changes, is the pathogenetic mechanism of diabetic neuropathy, and that the structural changes that occur in human diabetic neuropathies are similar to those in diabetic rat models, but are altered by superimposed factors that are specific to human diabetic neuropathic subtypes.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the mechanisms of diabetic neuropathy, and the clinical relevance of our research is that we have demonstrated that neuropathy in insulin dependent diabetes is a direct consequence of hyperglycemic injury, and that neuropathy in non- insulin dependent diabetes has a similar pathogenesis but is superimposed with additional ischemic and age-related effects.
the development of a mechanistic model of diabetic neuropathy, and the translation of this model from the diabetic rat to the human.
elucidating mechanisms of diabetic neuropathy, with a particular emphasis on the role of hyperglycemic-induced metabolic abnormalities.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the morphologic expression in diabetic neuropathy is heterogeneous and dependent on the type of diabetes, duration of hyperglycemic exposure, and age.
the morphological changes of diabetic neuropathy in the rat are reproduced in human neuropathy, but that the morphological expression is modified by the effects of non-glucose factors.

neuropathy in insulin-independent diabetes is a multifactorial process in which hyperglycemia is an important but not the sole factor, and that the morphological features of neuropathy in the two types of diabetes differ.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

in insulin-dependent diabetes, hyperglycemia directly causes axo-glial disruption and segmental demyeination, whereas in non-insulin-dependent patients, axo-glial damage is secondary to vascular ischemic injury.

the pathophysiological mechanisms of diabetic neuropathy are similar in both insulin-dependent and noninsulin-dependent diabetes, but that the morphological expression of these mechanisms is different.

the morphologic changes observed in the sural nerves of patients with diabetic neuropathy are consistent with the mechanistic model developed in the diabetic rat, but superimpose vascular, metabolic, hormonal and age-related effects which alter the expression of the neuropathic process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are multiple pathogenetic mechanisms in diabetic neuropathy.
there are multiple mechanisms for diabetic neuropathy, and the mechanisms may be quite different for type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
the pathogenesis of human diabetic neuropathy is multifactorial, and the morphologic expression is determined by the interplay of the various contributing pathogenetic factors.
